title: Ὁδοιπόροι καὶ κόραξ
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 255. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Πορευομένοις τισὶν ἐπὶ πρᾶξίν τινα κόραξ ὑπήντησε τὸν ἕτερον τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν πεπηρωμένος.
sentences.tr: Poreuomenois tisin epi praxin tina korax hypēntēse ton heteron tōn ophthalmōn pepērōmenos.
sentences.l: To certain men journeying upon some piece of business there came a raven to meet them, maimed in one of his two eyes.
sentences.i: Some men were on a journey about a piece of business when a raven met them, blinded in one of his eyes.
sentences.n: ὑπαντάω takes the dative of the person met, and that dative participle stands first in the sentence, carrying the whole circumstance before the subject arrives. τὸν ἕτερον τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν is an accusative of respect with the perfect participle — maimed 'as to one eye'; ἕτερος is one of a pair. A bird met on the road was a sign to be read, so the raven's state is not incidental.

sentences.t: Ἐπιστραφέντων δὲ αὐτῶν καί τινος ὑποστρέψαι παραινοῦντος, τοῦτο γὰρ σημαίνειν τὸν οἰωνόν, ἕτερος ὑποτυχὼν εἶπε· « Καὶ πῶς οὗτος ἡμῖν δύναται τὰ μέλλοντα μαντεύεσθαι, ὃς οὐδὲ τὴν ἰδίαν πήρωσιν προεῖδεν, ἵνα φυλάξηται ; »
sentences.tr: Epistraphentōn de autōn kai tinos hypostrepsai parainountos, touto gar sēmainein ton oiōnon, heteros hypotychōn eipe· « Kai pōs houtos hēmin dynatai ta mellonta manteuesthai, hos oude tēn idian pērōsin proeiden, hina phylaxētai ; »
sentences.l: And they having turned about, and one of them urging that they turn back — for that the omen meant this — another, taking-up-the-word, said: « And how can this one prophesy to us the things to come, who did not even foresee his own maiming, so as to guard against it? »
sentences.i: They turned round, and one of them urged that they go back, for that was what the omen meant; but another took up the word and said: « And how can this bird prophesy to us what is to come, when he did not even foresee his own blinding, so as to guard against it? »
sentences.n: ὑποτυχών is 'taking up the word, breaking in to answer', not a physical seizing — the house rendering across this corpus. The infinitive σημαίνειν after γάρ keeps the reason inside the first man's speech: it is his claim, reported, not the narrator's. οἰωνός is a bird considered as a sign, and so the sign itself. τὰ μέλλοντα, 'the things about to be', is the standing phrase for the future. ἵνα with the aorist middle subjunctive gives the purpose the foresight would have served.

sentences.t: Οὕτω καὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων οἱ ἐν τοῖς ἰδίοις ἄβουλοι καὶ εἰς τὰς τῶν πέλας συμβουλίας ἀδόκιμοί εἰσιν.
sentences.tr: Houtō kai tōn anthrōpōn hoi en tois idiois abouloi kai eis tas tōn pelas symboulias adokimoi eisin.
sentences.l: So too, among men, those who are without counsel in their own affairs are of no account for the counselling of their neighbours either.
sentences.i: So too, among men, those who have no judgement in their own affairs are worth nothing as advisers to anyone else.
sentences.n: ἀδόκιμος is what will not pass the assay — the word used of false coin. οἱ πέλας, 'those nearby', is the regular Greek for one's neighbours.
